name: Amira Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I deliver parcels through a flex app, which means I'm self-employed and I book blocks of three or four hours. Most days I collect from the sorting centre outside our market town at eight and drop about sixty parcels in my little hatchback, round the new estates and the older streets near the church. I've done it a year, after working in a shoe shop that closed. I'm engaged to Daniel, who's in the third year of an electrician apprenticeship, and we're saving for a small house.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not knowing if there'll be blocks next week wears me out, because it's all first come, first served on the app. Some weeks I get five days, some weeks two. What I like is being out in town, waving at people I know from church, and getting home in time for choir practice on a Wednesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because a lot of these big promises never come true. I'd say it after church, if anyone asked. I don't post much except the choir photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay as they are, and as they are is a bit shaky. The parcel blocks come and go, and I've no sick pay. But Daniel will be qualified in a year, and then we'll have one steady wage at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep booking blocks, and I'd set an alarm to grab them the minute they're released. I'd keep saving about a fifth of what I earn towards the house. I'd look at whether the sorting centre ever hires staff directly, because a contract would be steadier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit unsettled about the blocks, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a two-day week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cut the shopping back, we eat at my mum's on Sunday, and I don't put anything in the house savings that week. It's never a disaster, just a bit tight. Daniel says don't worry, but I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is saved towards the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four months of what we spend, between us. We'd want twice that for a deposit. So it's a long road, but we're on it.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because big promises often fail.
I'd mention it **after church** if asked, not online.
think: Things stay as they are, and that's **shaky**, with no **sick pay**.
Daniel **qualifies** in a year, giving us one steady wage.
do: Set an alarm to grab **flex blocks** the minute they're released.
Save about **a fifth** of earnings toward the house.
Ask whether the **sorting centre** hires staff directly.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit **unsettled** about the blocks.
S0.quote: The parcel blocks come and go, and I've no sick pay.
fieldNote: Her day-to-day worry is **irregular blocks** and no sick pay, not AI.
Her fiancé's **apprenticeship** is the household's coming anchor.
She'd look for a **direct contract**, a cautious step toward steadiness.

steps.text: Set an alarm to book flex blocks the moment they release
Put a fifth of earnings into the house savings
Ask the sorting centre about direct staff jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep calm and learn what's useful. I'd say it's office jobs that'll change most. I'd say families should help each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the app might get stricter, and more people from offices might grab the blocks. That could mean fewer weeks with five days for me. But my work is carrying parcels, so it's not the first thing to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, but I'd use the AI on my phone, which I sometimes use for the church newsletter, to work out the best times to grab blocks. I'd wait a bit before changing anything big. If blocks dropped a lot, I'd look at what Ruth from church did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Ruth from church do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth was a cleaner and did a teaching assistant course at the college, and now she works at the primary school. She loves it. If she can, maybe I could, but I'd want to see more people do it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Daniel's an electrician. Would his work change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel says he'll be busy fitting all the new machines, chargers and things. He's quite confident. I believe him, mostly.

say: I'd tell people to **keep calm** and learn what's useful.
I'd say **families** should help each other through the change.
think: More **office workers** might grab the flex blocks, so I'd get fewer full weeks.
My work is **carrying parcels**, so it's not the first to go.
do: Use the phone **AI** to find the best times to book blocks.
Look at Ruth's **teaching assistant** route if blocks drop a lot.
S1.quote: My work is carrying parcels, so it's not the first thing to go.
fieldNote: She sees **competition for blocks** as the main threat in this picture.
Her church friend's **teaching assistant** switch is her proven example.
She trusts her fiancé's **electrician** trade to stay busy.

steps.text: Use the phone AI to find the best times to book blocks
Watch how often she gets full weeks before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and families and churches will have to hold people together. I'd say we shouldn't just wait for the government. I'd pray about it, honestly, and I'd say that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the parcel blocks go by 2031, maybe earlier if the sorting centre gets robots. Daniel would probably still be busy wiring things, so we'd be all right on his wage, just slower. I'd be thirty-two and want to be doing something else by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the teaching assistant course in the first year, like Ruth. I'd keep doing parcel blocks around it. Daniel and I would probably bring the wedding forward and keep it small, so we're settled before things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sad, too, because I like being out in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want us married and settled before everything shifts. A small wedding at our church, family only. My mum would cry about the small part, but she'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't AI change teaching assistant work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the paperwork side. But children need someone to sit with them while they read. Ruth says the little ones need hugs. Little children need someone to tie their shoelaces, and I can't picture a robot doing that well.

say: I'd say it's **frightening**, and families and **churches** must hold people together.
I'd say we **shouldn't wait** for the government to fix it.
think: The **parcel blocks** go by 2031, maybe sooner with sorting robots.
Daniel's **electrician wage** would keep us going, just more slowly.
do: Start the **teaching assistant** course in the first year.
**Bring the wedding forward** and keep it small.
feel: **Anxious**, and **sad** to lose being out in town.
S2.quote: Little children need someone to tie their shoelaces, and I can't picture a robot doing that well.
fieldNote: She acts **sooner** here, choosing the proven teaching assistant route.
She leans on **church and family** rather than government.
Her fiancé's **trade** keeps the household from feeling desperate.

steps.text: Start the teaching assistant course at the college in year one
Bring the wedding forward as a small church ceremony
Lean on Daniel's electrician wage while she trains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, so families should talk about it now. I'd say young people should look at apprenticeships. I'd keep it hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about right for me. Daniel would be qualified and settled, and I could finish a course and get some experience. Robots by 2034 means the parcels last a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the parcel blocks for two or three years and save hard for the house. I'd start the teaching assistant course in year two, once I'd seen a couple more people do it. We'd have the wedding as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less so. It feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you save on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, mostly. We'd do a week at Daniel's aunt's by the sea instead of flying anywhere. And I'd stop buying coffee on the round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you it's time to switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the sorting centre starts testing robot vans, I'll know it's time to switch. Or when the app's blocks drop to three days a week for a month.

say: I'd say five years is **time to prepare**, so families should talk now.
I'd tell young people to look at **apprenticeships**.
think: Five years is **about right**: Daniel qualified, me retrained.
Robots by **2034** means parcels last a bit longer for me.
do: Keep **parcel blocks** for two or three years.
Save hard for the **house** by cutting holidays and coffees.
Start the **teaching assistant** course in year two.
S3.quote: When the sorting centre starts testing robot vans, I'll know it's time to switch.
fieldNote: She waits for **clear signals**, like robot trials at the sorting centre.
She still plans the **teaching assistant** route but later.
Her own job still **ends**, so she remains anxious despite the time.

steps.text: Save hard for the house deposit
Start the teaching assistant course in year two
Swap flying holidays for a week at Daniel's aunt's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and we should use it well. I'd say churches and families should prepare young people. I'd stay calm about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels comfortable. We'd be married, maybe with a baby, and Daniel would be a fully qualified electrician. I'd be thirty-nine when robots come for parcels, and by then I'd want to be at a school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the blocks for a few years and focus on the wedding and the house. I'd do the teaching assistant course in three or four years. We'd plan a baby without worrying too much about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. A small worry, far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait too long, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'm not one to rush. But I'd have Ruth reminding me, and Daniel, so I don't think I'd leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade or something with people, and don't rely on an app for your living. And go to church, because people there will look out for you.

I'd say churches and families should **prepare young people**.
think: Ten years feels **comfortable**: married, maybe a **baby**.
By **2039** I'd want to be working at a school.
do: Keep doing **blocks** while focusing on the wedding and house.
Take the **teaching assistant** course in three or four years.
Plan a **baby** without much worry about work.
S4.quote: Don't rely on an app for your living.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her put **family plans** first.
She expects friends and fiancé to **nudge** her to retrain in time.
Her advice to future children is **trade, people and church**.

steps.text: Keep booking parcel blocks for a few more years
Take the teaching assistant course in three or four years
Plan a baby with Daniel after the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would rush everything: the wedding, the course, the house. What would help is paid apprenticeships or courses for people like me, and the church and families doing what they do best, looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the self-employed side. I've no sick pay and no holiday pay now, and nobody talks about that. Before robots, I'd want that fixed for flex drivers.

headlineQuote: I've no sick pay and no holiday pay now, and nobody talks about that.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** self-employed parcel courier booking flex blocks in a market town.
She's **engaged** to Daniel, an electrician apprentice, and saving for a house.
She's **traditional**, leans on church and family, and waits for proof before changing.
Her **proven path** is a teaching assistant course, copying a friend from church.
She's **uneasy** in the slower pictures and anxious when AGI comes in 2028 or 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would rush the wedding, retraining and house all at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid courses** or apprenticeships for people like her.
**Sick pay** and holiday pay for self-employed flex drivers.
